name: Tocharian A
confidence_why: Malzahn 2010, Koller 2015 and Burlak & Itkin 2013 all state that the Tocharian A script gives no way to locate the accent, and Kim 2007, who tentatively places pre-Tocharian A primary stress on the first full vowel, himself concedes that little is known of Tocharian A accentuation.
catalog_citation: Malzahn, Melanie. 2010. The Tocharian Verbal System (Brill's Studies in Indo-European Languages & Linguistics 3). Leiden/Boston: Brill. Chapter 1 'Sound Laws', sec. 1.4 'Vowel Balance and Related Phenomena in Tocharian A', pp. 8-10. Secondary: Krause, Todd B.…
catalog_locator: Malzahn 2010 pp. 8-10 (sec. 1.4); LRC Tocharian Online lesson-10 page, Series Introduction sec. 1.4
catalog_quote: Whereas the location of the accent in Tocharian B can be detected on the basis of the different renderings of /ä/ and /a/, no such device is available for establishing the synchronic accent rules of Tocharian A. Consequently, there are different views on the synchronic accent of Tocharian A. However, most scholars work with the hypothesis that the accent rules of pre-Tocharian A at least were the same as the ones found valid for Tocharian B, i.e., that one can reconstruct the accent system of Proto-Tocharian on the basis of Tocharian B alone. ... Since in the context of vowel balance a full vowel never undergoes any kind of weakening in an initial syllable, it is rather safe to assume that in Tocharian A full vowels implementing the peak of an initial syllable in a word bore the accent.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Malzahn 2010 text we hold at pp. 8 and 10 (sec. 1.4), elision correctly marked; p. 9 exceptions quote and the LRC sec. 1.4 secondary quote also verbatim. (2) Deciding source: a 2010 specialist monograph (historical-phonology chapter) by a leading Tocharologist -- not a dedicated accent study, but authoritative; the language is extinct and its Brahmi orthography gives no accent diagnostic, so not determinable is the field consensus, not an artefact of a weak source. (3) downloaded now, all open and Burlak & Itkin 2013 (46-pp Jazyki mira grammar sketch of TA, p. 401: no indications of stress or tone in the written record) -- confirms; Koller 2015 UCLA diss. p. 85 'our very limited knowledge of TA accent' -- confirms; Kim 2007 pp. 9, 26 'we know little about TA accentuation', hyp

sources.quote: p. 85: 'It appears that this enclitic [oki] was not necessarily unaccented, but could attract the accent of its host. sources.quote: p. 9: 'Although we know little about TA accentuation, it seems probable that the position of stress played a role in this bifurcation: if we assume that primary stress fell on the first "full vowel" (see sec. 6)...'. p. 26: 'It is tempting to suppose that primary stress in pre-TA came to fall on the first full vowel, with secondary stress following two syllables after; thus the stress pattern in such forms was *V́ V V̀ ... The raising of *ā > *a after a primary stressed syllable, and further raising of *a > *ä between stressed syllables, would then be phonetically most natural.'

sources.note: 'ton' here is the inherited Indo-European (pitch) accent; an 8-page comparative note relating IE accent ('ton') to the Tocharian vowel reflexes, i.e. accent-conditioned vocalism in the prehistory of Tocharian A and B. It is the one tone-titled item in the Tocharian literature; it is not expected to claim lexical tone for attested Tocharian A. Print only (Klincksieck 1978).
